quote: Probleme, wie die Frage, ob es eine Fläche $4^{\text{ter}}$ Ordnung mit 11 getrennten Ovalen giebt, oder ob welches die Maximalzahl der sich einander umschliessenden Züge einer ebenen
english: Problems such as the question whether there exists a surface of 4th order with 11 separate ovals, or what the maximum number of mutually enclosing branches of a plane [curve is] (sentence continues on the next page).
topic: The page finishes an argument that every form near a form expressible as a sum of 2n-th powers of linear forms with positive coefficients is itself so expressible, then sets out a plan to prove the prime number theorem by systematically solving Chebyshev's functional equation, and begins a remark on problems such as quartic surfaces with 11 ovals.

triage.modern_statement: This is the material Hilbert later posed as the first part of his 16th Paris problem (1900), on the topology of real algebraic curves and surfaces. (a) Can a smooth real quartic surface in RP^3 have 11 connected components ('ovals' or 'sheets')? Equivalently, what is the largest number of components a real quartic surface can have? Rohn (1886) had shown it is at most 12. (b) The fragment that runs onto the next page asks for the largest number of nested ovals (mutually enclosing branches) a real plane curve of degree n can have. More broadly, it asks how the ovals of a curve with the maximal number of branches can be arranged.
triage.answered_by: Quartic surfaces: V. M. Kharlamov proved in 1972 (Funktsional. Anal. i Prilozhen.) that a real quartic surface in RP^3 has at most 10 components, so no quartic with 11 ovals exists, and 10 is the maximum. Kharlamov finished the full classification of nonsingular real quartic surfaces by 1976. Related work on plane curves: Gudkov solved the sextic-curve part in 1969, and Rokhlin's formula settled Hilbert's conjectures about the 11 ovals of plane sextics.

evidence.claim: Kharlamov solved the quartic-surface part of Hilbert's 16th problem in 1972. The maximum number of components of a real quartic surface in 3-space is 10, not the bound of 12 that Rohn proved in 1886, which was the best known in 1900.

In the 16th problem Hilbert says the maximum number of sheets of a surface of order 4 was not yet known (citing Rohn 1886). Today we know the maximum number of connected components of a quartic surface in projective 3-space is 10, and Kharlamov completed the study of nonsingular quartic surfaces by 1976.

The 16th problem asks for a thorough investigation of how the branches of curves with the maximal number of branches are arranged, and asks the same about the sheets of surfaces, including the maximum number of sheets of a quartic surface.
Rokhlin's formula settles two of Hilbert's conjectures on the 11 ovals of plane sextics, which Hilbert included in his 16th problem.
The first part of the 16th problem (the topology of real plane curves) is still unsolved for degree 8.

triage.why: The note matches the wording of Hilbert's 16th problem: a surface of order 4 with 11 separate ovals or sheets (Rohn's open question), together with the arrangement and nesting of ovals of plane curves. The quartic-surface question has been answered: Kharlamov showed in 1972 that the maximum is 10, so a quartic with 11 ovals does not exist. The nested-ovals question breaks off at the page boundary, and the sources I found don't address the maximum nesting depth directly, so I can't say exactly what Hilbert asked or how it was resolved. Within the curve classification problem it belongs to, the sextic case was settled (Gudkov 1969; Rokhlin's formula), but the classification is open from degree 8 on and is still an active area of research in real algebraic geometry.
